label: Greeted by name
reason: The outcome that the claim names: a reply that opens with the name of the sender.
estimates: Whether a reply opens with the name of the sender, in any form from "Hi Brett" to "Dear Ms. Martinez".
explanation: The claim is about tone, and the original authors measure tone by whether the official greets the sender by name, coded leniently so that any named salutation counts. It is the outcome of every analysis on the curve.

label: Any reply
reason: A different claim of the same paper, about whether officials reply at all.
estimates: Whether the email drew any reply from the housing authority.
explanation: Whether officials reply at all is the first outcome of the paper, which finds equal reply rates for Black and white names and only a small, uncertain gap for Hispanic names. It answers a question about access rather than tone, so it is taught beside the curve rather than on it.

label: Reply within 24 hours
reason: A different claim, about the speed of replies among those who replied.
estimates: Whether a reply, when one came, arrived within 24 hours of the email.
explanation: Speed is the second measure of responsiveness in the paper, and it shows no gap by the name of the sender. It is another question about access, kept off the curve of the tone claim.

label: White names
reason: The comparison that the claim as SCORE selected it names: Hispanic against white names.
estimates: The difference between emails signed with Hispanic names and emails signed with white names.
explanation: The sentence that SCORE selected reads "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts", so the comparison with white names answers it word for word. It leaves the emails with Black names out of the analysis.

label: White and Black names
reason: The comparison of the abstract, which sets Hispanic names against "black and white counterparts".
estimates: The difference between emails signed with Hispanic names and all other emails, signed with white or Black names.
explanation: The abstract of the paper compares Hispanic applicants with their "black and white counterparts", and the ellipsis in the sentence that SCORE selected removed the word 'black'. Pooling the two comparison groups answers the abstract as written, and it is the comparison of one of the five analysts.

label: Black names
reason: A different claim, about Black rather than Hispanic names.
estimates: The difference between emails signed with Black names and emails signed with white names.
explanation: The paper reports no significant gap in greetings between Black and white names; its main finding on the Black names is that they drew replies as often as the white names. It is a separate claim, taught beside the curve.

label: Replies only
reason: The rows of the paper: the share of greetings among the emails that drew a reply.
phrase: among the emails that drew a reply
estimates: The difference in the share of replies that open with a name, among the emails that drew a reply.
explanation: This is the comparison that the paper reports and the one that four of the five analysts made. Because the name of the sender may also change whether an official replies at all, the replies to Hispanic and to white names need not come from comparable officials, so this difference describes the replies rather than measuring a pure effect of the name.

label: All delivered emails
reason: Every delivered email, with no reply counted as no greeting, which keeps the comparison randomised.
phrase: among all delivered emails, a missing reply counting as no greeting
estimates: The difference in the share of emails that drew a reply opening with a name, among all delivered emails.
explanation: Counting every email that reached an official keeps the two groups exactly as randomisation made them, so the difference is an effect of the name on receiving a named greeting. The original authors mention this version in a footnote, saying that it does not affect the results, and one of the five analysts made it the main analysis; it gives a smaller gap, because fewer than six in ten emails drew any reply.

label: Male and female names
reason: The claim pools the male and the female name of each group, as the paper does.
phrase: with male and female names pooled
estimates: The difference averaged over the male and the female name of each group.
explanation: The paper consolidates the two names of each group, and the claim speaks of Hispanic applicants in general. Pooling keeps every email in the analysis.

label: Male names only
reason: A subgroup: Santiago against Brett, a narrower question that the SCORE replication also asked.
estimates: The difference between Santiago and Brett alone.
explanation: The male names show the larger gap in the original data, and the SCORE replication used male names only. A subgroup answers a narrower question than the claim, about men, so it stays off the curve.

label: Female names only
reason: A subgroup: Gabriela against Emily, a narrower question than the claim.
estimates: The difference between Gabriela and Emily alone.
explanation: The female names show a smaller gap that is close to the edge of significance. A subgroup answers a narrower question than the claim, about women, so it stays off the curve.

label: Any official
reason: Every reply counts, whoever wrote it.
estimates: The difference over all replies, whoever wrote them.
explanation: Who replies is decided after the email arrives, so any selection on it can undo the randomisation. Keeping every reply is the only choice that does not select on what happened after the name was assigned.

label: Officials with Hispanic names
reason: A different question, about representative bureaucracy, asked on a selection that happens after the email arrives.
estimates: The difference among the replies written by officials whose names are distinctively Hispanic.
explanation: The paper asks whether Hispanic officials treat Hispanic applicants better, which is a separate hypothesis. Who replies is itself a consequence of the email, and the subgroup holds only a few dozen replies, so the comparison is fragile on two counts.

label: Leave out
reason: The five replies without a greeting code are left out, as most analysts did.
phrase: leaving out the replies without a greeting code
estimates: The share computed over the replies that carry a greeting code.
explanation: Five replies in the file have no greeting code. Leaving them out is what a model does by default, and it is what four of the five analysts did.

label: Count as no greeting
reason: The five replies count as replies without a greeting, as one analysis did by keeping the three of them that went to white and Hispanic names in the denominators.
phrase: counting the replies without a greeting code as no greeting
estimates: The share computed over every reply, with the five uncoded replies counted as replies that do not open with a name.
explanation: If the coders could find no greeting, the reply probably did not open with a name, which is a defensible reading. One of the five analysts made this choice without stating it, by keeping the three of them that went to white and Hispanic names in the count of emails.

label: Leave out
reason: Bounced emails never reached an official, so they are outside the experiment.
phrase: leaving out the emails that bounced
estimates: Every comparison over the emails that reached a housing authority.
explanation: Twenty-three emails bounced and have no reply status. They never reached an official, so the name on them cannot have changed anything, and every analysis on the curve leaves them out.

label: Count as no reply
reason: Counts emails that no official received as unanswered, which mixes a failure of delivery into the outcome.
phrase: counting the emails that bounced as unanswered
estimates: The comparison over every email sent, with a bounced email counted as an email without a reply.
explanation: Treating a bounced email as an unanswered one adds rows whose outcome was settled by a broken address rather than by an official. It answers the claim less well than leaving them out.

label: Difference in proportions
reason: A linear model of a 0/1 outcome, whose coefficient is the difference in percentage points.
phrase: a linear probability model (a difference in proportions)
estimates: The difference between the two shares, in percentage points, adjusted for covariates when there are any.
explanation: Without covariates the linear probability model is the difference between the two observed shares, the plainest answer to the claim. Its errors are taken with the HC2 correction, which suits a 0/1 outcome and a randomised comparison.

label: Logistic regression
reason: The model of the paper, reported on the course scale as an average marginal effect.
phrase: a logistic regression, reported as an average marginal effect
estimates: The difference in the predicted probability of a greeting, averaged over the analysed emails, from a logistic model.
explanation: The original authors and three of the analysts fitted logistic regressions. Converted into the average change in the probability of a greeting, the logit answers on the same scale as the linear model and, without covariates, gives exactly the same difference.

label: Three-group model
reason: The same contrast fitted with all three groups in the model, as the original authors did; a check of the two-group fit.
phrase: a model with all three groups of names
estimates: The contrast of Hispanic with white names inside a model that also holds the emails with Black names.
explanation: Fitting all three groups at once lets the emails with Black names inform the covariates, which changes the estimate only slightly. It is how the original authors and two of the analysts fitted the model, and the course uses it as a check.

label: No covariates
reason: Randomisation makes covariates unnecessary for an unbiased comparison.
estimates: The raw difference between the groups.
explanation: Because the names were assigned at random, the groups of housing authorities differ only by chance, and the raw difference answers the claim without adjustment.

label: Hard-to-find address
reason: Adds whether the address had to be taken from the HUD list, which predicts replies.
estimates: The difference holding constant whether the email address of the authority was hard to find.
explanation: Covariates in an experiment buy precision, not unbiasedness. The hard-to-find address predicts replies and greetings, so adding it can narrow the uncertainty slightly.

label: Place, without ethnic composition
reason: Adds the size and the poverty of the community in thirds, the set that the Multi100 instruction leaves.
phrase: adjusting for the address, and the size and poverty of the community
estimates: The difference holding constant the hard-to-find address and the thirds of population and poverty rate.
explanation: The second Multi100 task told the analysts to "disregard the moving locations' ethnical composition", which leaves size and poverty. The thirds come from the public file, which replaces the continuous census values to protect the authorities.

label: Place, with ethnic composition
reason: The covariates of the original model, in the thirds that the public file holds.
phrase: adjusting for the address and the size, poverty and ethnic composition of the community
estimates: The difference holding constant the hard-to-find address and the thirds of population, poverty, percent Black and percent Hispanic.
explanation: These are the covariates of Table 1 of the paper, in the form that the public file allows. The original authors' blinded code fits exactly this set.

label: Sex of the name
reason: Adds the sex of the name, which the design balances, so it changes almost nothing; a check.
phrase: adjusting for the sex of the name
estimates: The difference holding constant whether the name was male or female.
explanation: Each group has one male and one female name, so the sex of the name is balanced by design. One analyst adjusted for it; the course keeps it as a check.

label: Continuous census values
reason: The continuous census covariates of the paper are not in the public file, because they would identify the authorities.
phrase: adjusting for the continuous census values
estimates: The difference holding constant the continuous 2012 ACS values of the community.
explanation: The paper adjusts for the continuous percentages and the logged population, but the public file holds only thirds of them, because the exact values would identify the housing authorities. No one outside the original team can fit the published model exactly, which is why its reproduction is approximate by design.

label: The test of the model
reason: HC2 errors for the linear model, the usual z test for the logit: the rule of the curve.
phrase: the test of the model (HC2 errors for the linear model)
estimates: A two-sided test at the 5% level of the coefficient of the Hispanic names.
explanation: Each specification is tested by its own model, which is what a single analyst would report. The randomisation test of every specification is stored beside it as a check.

label: Randomisation test
reason: Reshuffles the names among the analysed emails; stored for every specification as a check.
estimates: How often a random reshuffling of the names gives a gap as large as the observed one.
explanation: The randomisation test needs no model of the errors, only the fact that the names were assigned at random. It agrees with the model tests on every specification of the curve.

label: Chi-square test
reason: The test of a two-by-two table, with the continuity correction that R applies by default; a check.
phrase: a chi-square test of the two-by-two table
estimates: Whether the share of greetings differs between the two groups, without a model.
explanation: One analyst tested the claim with a chi-square test of the table of names against greetings. It tests the same difference without a model; the continuity correction, which R applies to a two-by-two table unless told otherwise, makes it slightly more conservative.

label: One-tailed test
reason: Halves the p-value by deciding the direction in advance; the paper uses it once, for replies.
estimates: A test that counts only a gap in the predicted direction.
explanation: The paper calls the gap in replies "borderline significant (with a one-tailed test)". A one-tailed test is defensible only if the direction was fixed before the data were seen, so the curve keeps two-sided tests.

label: Percentage points
reason: The scale of the claim: the paper speaks of "twenty percentage points".
estimates: The difference in the share of greetings, in percentage points.
explanation: The abstract of the paper states the gap in percentage points, which a reader can picture without a formula. Every point of the curve is placed on this scale.

label: Odds ratio
reason: The logit coefficient on its own scale; it changes when covariates are added even in an experiment.
estimates: The ratio of the odds of a greeting for Hispanic names to the odds for white names.
explanation: Odds ratios are what a logistic regression reports, but they shift when covariates are added even under randomisation, because they are not averages over the analysed emails. The course reports the logit on the percentage-point scale instead.

label: Partial correlation
reason: The scale on which Multi100 put every reanalysis, so that tests of different kinds can be compared.
estimates: The test statistic converted into a correlation by the rules of Multi100.
explanation: Multi100 converted each reported test into a correlation, with the sample size standing in for the degrees of freedom of a z test. The conversion makes different tests comparable, but its size depends on the number of emails analysed as well as on the gap.
